tier_reason: The gist run_bench.py (coleifer, the author of the unqlite-python binding) times UnQLite against Python sqlite3 and prints 1.054 s / 1.353 s for UnQLite and 6.977 s / 1.890 s for SQLite at N = 100,000, but states no hardware, library versions, compiler or flags and runs each test once, so it is informal evidence below A and not a recognised suite (not B). Tier stays C; the verdict is downgrade because the 6.6x write ratio is not a like-for-like measurement.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Reads: UnQLite 1.35 s vs SQLite 1.89 s for 100,000 single-key lookups through the Python bindings, about 1.4x faster (derived from page data). Writes: UnQLite 1.05 s vs SQLite 6.98 s (6.6x, derived from page data), but this ratio is not like-for-like: SQLite commits every row inside the timed loop while UnQLite's writes stay in its implicit transaction, which is committed only at close, outside the timed region. Same table: LevelDB 0.38 s / 0.31 s, Kyoto Cabinet B-tree 0.27 s / 0.28 s, GDBM 0.29 s / 0.17 s, BDB B-tree 0.95 s / 0.69 s, so UnQLite is not the fastest embedded store in this run.
corrections.caveats: Informal evidence: a one-file Python 2 script (gist by coleifer, who also maintains the unqlite-python binding; gist last active 2 Sep 2020, creation date not shown) run once per engine with no stated hardware, OS, library versions, compiler or flags. Write timings are not comparable: the SQLite test calls commit() after every INSERT inside the timed loop (one durable transaction per row, no WAL or PRAGMA tuning), while the UnQLite test only assigns db[i] = i and never commits; UnQLite's default is auto-commit on close (unqlite.c: UNQLITE_FL_DISABLE_AUTO_COMMIT 'Disable auto-commit on close'; unqliteDbRelease commits the outstanding transaction), and the script closes the database after both timings, so UnQLite's commit and fsync cost is excluded. The 1.4x read gap is the only fair figure, and it includes Python binding overhead (SQLite reads also run a SQL SELECT plus fetchall per key). The script's RocksDB read method has no return statement (the page does not comment on this). unqlite.org and unqlite.symisc.net did not resolve from this environment; the repo README carries no benchmarks. The two UnQLite seed lines are the same project, filed as one record.

notes: Numbers on the gist match the record. Shortcomings to record: write ratio excludes UnQLite's commit (auto-commit on close happens outside the timed region) while SQLite fsyncs per row; read win only 1.4x; single run, no hardware/versions; benchmark author maintains the UnQLite Python binding; several other stores (LevelDB, Kyoto, GDBM) beat UnQLite in the same table. Metadata checked: BSD-2-Clause, 2.3k stars, 181 forks, last commit 2026-09-05 (active).

tier_reason: First-party homepage claim (about 90x faster than LevelDB v1.11.0 and 140x faster than BerkeleyDB v5.1.0 on a 50-million-record max scan, 4 MB cache, 64-bit Linux), confirmed only through a WebSearch snippet of upscaledb.com; the linked benchmark code (gist benchmark.cc + Makefile) is public but has no results, no CPU model, and builds the driver at -O0 with library flags unstated, and the >50x gain caps it at C anyway.

corrections.caveats: Snippet only: upscaledb.com did not resolve from this environment (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND); a site-restricted WebSearch snippet of the homepage confirms the claim: full-table scan over 50 million records retrieving the maximum, upscaledb about 90 times faster than leveldb and about 140 times faster than BerkeleyDB, upscaledb v2.0.0, leveldb v1.11.0, BerkeleyDB v5.1.0, 64-bit Linux, 4 MB cache, with a link to the benchmark code. That code is the author's gist (https://gist.github.com/cruppstahl/dd98144e52ceac2e1df06df1fe7b852b, created 2016-04-04, one run per test, no results): upscaledb computes the max with its built-in query uqi_select('MAX($record) FROM DATABASE 1') inside the B+tree, while Berkeley DB and LevelDB walk every record with a cursor/iterator and track the max in driver code compiled with g++ -std=c++11 -g -O0, so the baselines' per-record loop runs unoptimized while upscaledb's runs in the optimized library; flags for the three libraries are not stated, no absolute timings or CPU model are published, LevelDB uses its default bytewise comparator on raw uint32 bytes with compression off, and the gist prints but does not exit on wrong results. Versions date from 2014-2016; the repo's last commit is 2021-08-20 and its README and ChangeLog carry no benchmarks. Per search snippets, a 2014-era hamsterdb-vs-leveldb post by the same author was mixed (hamsterdb faster on random reads and sequential inserts/scans, slower on random writes past about 10 million keys). The Lemire and Rupp paper (arXiv 1611.05428) was not reachable and compares codecs inside upscaledb only.

notes: Homepage numbers confirmed by snippet only (vendor site blocked); tier C stands (first-party, no CPU model, >50x with unstated library flags). Shortcomings to record: not like-for-like (built-in MAX vs full iteration), baseline loop compiled at -O0, no absolute timings or hardware, 2014-2016 versions, project abandoned (last commit 2021-08-20). Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, 572 stars, 70 forks, not archived.
